titleStmt.title: A Generic Framework for Soft Real-Time Program Executions on NAND Flash Memory in Multi-Tasking Embedded Systems

analytic.title: A Generic Framework for Soft Real-Time Program Executions on NAND Flash Memory in Multi-Tasking Embedded Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper proposes a novel technique called mRT-PLRU (Multi-tasking Real-Time constrained combination of Pinning and LRU), which forms a generic framework to use inexpensive nonvolatile NAND flash memory for storing and executing real-time programs in multi-tasking environments. In order to execute multiple real-time tasks stored in NAND flash memory with the minimal usage of expensive RAM, the mRT-PLRU is optimally configured in two steps. In the first step, the per-task analysis finds the function of RAM size vs. execution time for each individual task. Using these functions for all the tasks as inputs, the second-step called a stochastic-analysis-in-loop optimization conducts an iterative convex optimization with the stochastic-analysis for the probabilistic schedulability check. As a result, the optimization loop can optimally allocate RAM to multiple tasks such that their deadlines are probabilistically guaranteed with the minimal usage of RAM. Moreover, the mRT-PLRU is optimally configured in a developer-transparent way without giving any burden to the program developer, which is essential for the embedded system industry under a high pressure of time-to-market. The usefulness of the developed technique is intensively verified through both simulation and actual implementation. Our experimental study shows that mRT-PLRU can save up to 80% of RAM required by the industry-common shadowing approach.

div.head: I. Introduction
div.p: NAND flash memory has been widely used for mobile embedded systems such as cellular phones, portable media players, and personal navigators, due to its nonvolatility, shock resistance, and low-power consumption. NAND flash memory, however, has challenging physical characteristics such as page-based read/write operations, long delay for a write operation, erase-before-write requirements, and limited erase counts. Especially, the fact that a read operation is performed only on 2KB pagebasis-byte-level random accesses are not allowed 1 , makes it impossible to execute program codes directly from NAND flash memory. Thus, the most commonly used approach in the industry is shadowing [25] that copies the entire program codes in NAND flash memory into RAM and executes them from RAM. However, this approach requires a large amount of RAM, which sacrifices the price benefit of NAND flash memory. In order to run programs in NAND flash memory with a smaller RAM, [18] proposes a NAND-based demand-paging mechanism that reads pages into RAM when they are actually accessed while replacing pages as needed. However, due to unpredictable page-faults, this approach does not provide any real-time guarantee of program executions.

Therefore, the mobile embedded system industry needs a framework for executing program codes in NAND flash memory satisfying the program's real-time requirements with minimal usage of RAM. Our previous technique called RT-PLRU (Real-Time constrained combination of Pinning and LRU-based demand paging) [12] minimizes the RAM size under real-time constraints by optimally combining (1)Pinning-preload NAND pages and keep them in RAM and (2) LRU-based Demand-Paging-read NAND pages into RAM when accessed while replacing existing pages using the LRU (Least-Recently-Used) policy. However, the technique was developed under the assumption that only a single task is running targeting for a portable media player.

In many practical applications, there are great needs for executing multiple real-time tasks concurrently. A 3G mobile phone that can host multi-party video phone calls is a typical example of such a multi-tasking system, since video/voice encoders and decoders need to run concurrently meeting real-time constraints. In order to form a general framework for using NAND flash memory for multi-tasking real-time applications, this paper proposes a novel technique called mRT-PLRU (Multi-tasking RT-PLRU) that makes multiple real-time tasks optimally use RAM so that they can probabilistically guarantee their deadlines with the minimal requirement of total RAM size. The technique consists of two steps. In the first step so called a per-task analysis, we investigate each task's NAND page access pattern to find the function of "RAM size vs. optimal execution time (and the corresponding optimal PLRU)". Using those functions found for all the tasks, in the second step, we perform a special convex optimization called a stochastic-analysis-in-loop optimization that iteratively increases RAM allocations to tasks in a way of minimizing the total RAM size until the stochasticanalysis says that all the tasks can satisfy the deadline meet probability requirements.

Another important goal of our proposed technique is developer-transparency, that is, it must give no extra burden to the program developer, which is essential for the industry under a high pressure of time-to-market. For this, mRT-PLRU is configured by our automated kernel configurator without asking program source files and special probing functions from the program developer.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: The next section presents a brief background on NAND flash memory and formal description of our problem. In Section III, we propose a new approach to optimally configuring mRT-PLRU for multi-tasking systems. Section IV presents the experimental results through both trace-driven simulations and actual implementations. Section V briefly surveys the related work. Finally, Section VI concludes this paper.

div.head: II. Background and problem description
div.p: A NAND flash memory chip consists of a number of blocks as shown in Figure 1. Typically, each block has 64 pages where each page consists of 2 KBytes main area and 64 Bytes spare area [22]. The main area is used to store regular information such as program codes/data while

div.head: Fig. 2. Memory system architecture of NANDbased embedded systems
div.p: the spare area is used for storing auxiliary information such as error correction codes (ECC) and page-mapping information. Each page is read or written through an one-page size internal register (i.e., main register + spare register). Related to this internal structure, NAND flash memory exhibits challenging characteristics: (1) 2KB page based read/write, i.e., no byte-level random access, (2) long delay write, and (3) erase before write with even a longer delay and an erase count limit.

These characteristics make it hard to execute programs directly from NAND flash memory. Therefore, we have to use RAM as a working storage for executing programs as shown in Figure 2. Noting that the per-byte price of RAM is at least 10 times more expensive than that of NAND flash memory, we need to minimize the required RAM size to reduce the unit cost of production.

If we preload and keep (i.e., "pin") all the NAND pages into RAM, which is called the shadowing approach, the actual program execution does not incur any NAND read time. However, it requires one RAM page for every NAND page resulting in a huge RAM cost. As the other extreme, if we on-demand read (i.e., "demand-paging") all the NAND pages into a single RAM page, it causes frequent page faults whenever the program tries to access codes and data in a different NAND page. Thus, tasks frequently miss their deadlines. Our problem is how to optimally combine pinning and demand-paging for all the tasks such that the total RAM size is minimized while probabilistically guaranteeing task deadlines. Problem Description: With the above motivation in mind, our problem is specifically described in the following. We are given a set of n periodic tasks
div.formula: Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , • • • , τ n }. Each task τ i is characterized by a 4-tuple (C i , p i , D i , P rob th i )
div.p: . C i denotes the program that the task τ i executes at every period. p i denotes the period of τ i . D i denotes the relative deadline of τ i . The j-th execution of τ i is called the j-th job of τ i and denoted by J ij . Each job should complete before its deadline with a probability higher than a threshold P rob th i . The given set of n periodic tasks are scheduled by a fixed priority scheduling algorithm where τ i has a higher priority than τ j if i < j.

If the given n tasks share the entire RAM, they conflict each other when accessing RAM and hence their execution behavior becomes totally unpredictable. Therefore, we consider a partitioning approach where each task is assigned with a dedicated partition of RAM.
Under this task set and probabilistic temporal constraints, our problem is to answer the following questions for every task τ i in Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , • • • , τ n }:
• How many RAM pages need to be allocated to τ i ?

The number of RAM pages, i.e., the RAM partition size, allocated to τ i is denoted by S i . • Out of S i pages allocated to τ i , how many pages need to be used for pinning the pages of C i ? The number of RAM pages to be used for pinning is denoted by S pinning i . We also have to answer which S pinning i pages of C i need to be pinned.
div.formula: τ i ∈ {τ 1 , τ 2 , • • • , τ n }, that is, minimize n i=1 S i subject to dmp i ≥ P rob th i for all τ i ∈ Γ
div.p: where dmp i is the deadline meet probability of τ i . When solving the above optimization problem, we assume that only the executable file of the program C i is given without requiring any extra inputs such as source codes and special probing functions from the programmer. Thus, our method is implemented in an automated kernel configurator consisting of the "kernel-level profiler" running in a target board and the "on-host optimizer" running in a host computer. The kernel-level profiler collects execution traces by pre-running the given executable file and the collected traces are directed to the on-host optimizer that automatically finds the optimal solution, without expecting any assistance from the program developer-"developertransparent" approach.

The given executable file of program C i of task τ i consists of code part (.text) with m c i NAND pages and data part (.data and .bss) with m d i NAND pages as shown in Figure 3. The data part including global and static variables are updated frequently while the program is executing. Thus, if they reside in NAND flash memory, it requires many long-delay write operations which in turn cause even more expensive erase operations. Thus, it is necessary to statically bind the m d i data pages to RAM so that frequent writes are performed on RAM rather than NAND flash memory.

On the other hand, m c i code pages are read-only and thus they can either be pinned or demand-paged. Thus, in the rest of this paper, we focus on m c i code pages when finding the optimal combination of pinning and demandpaging.

div.head: III. Developer transparent mRT-PLRU configuration for a multi-tasking system
div.p: In order to optimally configure mRT-PLRU targeting for a multi-tasking system, the following two types of intertask conflicts should be addressed.

• Inter-task conflicts in RAM: If RAM is shared by multiple concurrent tasks, pages loaded into RAM by one task can be evicted by another. • Inter-task conflicts in processor: In a multi-tasking environment, high priority tasks can delay the executions of low priority ones. The first conflict can be avoided by partitioning RAM and allocating partitions to tasks for their dedicated use. However, the second conflict prevents us from using the previous way of RT-PLRU configuration that assumes a single task and trades its sleep times for reducing the RAM size. Therefore, we propose a new method to find the optimal RT-PLRUs for multiple tasks, which is called mRT-PLRU (Multi-tasking Real-Time constrained combination of Pinning and LRU), that satisfies the deadline meet probability requirements of all the tasks. For the developer transparency, in the learning phase, our kernel configurator automatically finds the mRT-PLRU with two steps: (1) per-task analysis and ( 2) stochastic-analysis-inloop optimization.

div.head: A. Step 1: per-task analysis
div.p: In the per-task analysis step, we analyze each task one by one by pre-running it on a prototype system equipped with a large enough RAM. Let us explain this step using a task τ i without loss of generality.

With the given executable file C i for task τ i , we preload all the program codes into RAM, that is, shadowing the program codes. Then, we run it with a sample input data stream until a large enough number of jobs are executed. We denote that number of jobs by L. During this shadowing-based pre-running of C i , our kernel-level profiler measures the execution time et ij of each job J ij . The execution time et ij is the time that J ij takes until completion under the condition of zero page fault and zero delay by other tasks. After that, we run the executable file once again with the same input data stream to trace the page reference sequence of each job. For this, our kernel-level profiler keeps only one valid page in RAM by invalidating previous pages every time a new NAND page is loaded. This causes a page-fault every time the program's control moves across one page boundary. div.head: B. Step 2: stochastic-analysis-in-loop optimization
div.p: With avgE i (S i ) functions and associated data for all the tasks given by the per-task analysis, our on-host optimizer conducts an optimization process. This optimization process tries to allocate minimum possible RAM to the tasks under the constraint that the deadline meet probability dmp i of each task τ i is greater than or equal to the deadline meet probability threshold P rob th i . The optimization is fundamentally based on the discrete convex optimization as in Q-RAM work [20], [14]. That is, with avgE i (S i ) functions as convex guidelines, it increases S i values in a way of meeting all the P rob th i requirements as quickly as possible-minimum increase of total RAM size, i.e., n i=1 S i . However, unlike the traditional convex optimization that assumes a resource budget for the termination condition, we do not have such a budget that guarantees the probabilistic deadline requirements. In order to tackle this challenge, we propose a stochastic-analysisin-loop optimization that uses the stochastic-analysis [8] to J 11 J 12 J 13 J 14

The stochastic-analysis proposed in [8] takes the execution time distributions E 1 , E 2 , • • • , E n as inputs and computes the response time distributions R 1 , R 2 , • • • , R n as outputs, as shown in Figure 5 for a two task example. From the computed response time distribution R i of each task τ i , we can simply calculate the deadline meet probability of τ i by summing up the probabilities that the response time is smaller than or equal to the deadline D i . The research on the stochastic-analysis says that the average system utilization is the most important factor that determines the deadline meet probabilities. That is, there is a strong tendency that if the average system utilization is small, the deadline meet probabilities are high for all the tasks. Thus, our optimization tries to maximally reduce the average utilization for the same increase of RAM in order to meet all P rob th i requirements with the smallest possible increase of n i=1 S i . div.head: IV. Experiments
div.p: This section justifies the proposed approach through both trace-driven simulation and actual implementation. As a prototype system used in the learning phase, we use Samsung Q1UMPC equipped with Intel A110 800Mhz processor, 64 GByte NAND flash memory and 1GByte RAM as shown in Figure 8. On top of this prototype system, we implement the kernel-level profiler by modifying the Linux kernel 2.6.24.7. As a typical multi-tasking soft real-time application, we consider a mobile video phone scenario where the video decoder and encoder tasks should run concurrently. For the video decoder and encoder programs, we use H.264 decoder/encoder made by ITU-T Joint Video Team. When the two tasks are concurrently running, they are scheduled by the fixed-priority scheduling with the decoder task having a higher priority. Also, we assume 24 fps video streaming and hence the periods for both decoder and encoder tasks are 41.6 ms. Their deadlines are assumed to be the same as the periods, since we can avoid frame dropping if a job completes within a period.

Since the page size from Linux's perspective is 4KB, from now on, by a page, we mean a 4KB page, which is Our rule of thumb regarding the deadline meet probability threshold P rob th is 95% for both decoder and encoder tasks to ensure that human cannot perceive any quality distortion of the video playback. Thus, we use 95% as the default value of P rob th for all the tasks unless otherwise mentioned.

In our learning phase, as a sample content, we use a 42-second sample content consisting of 1000 video frames where a student Kangwook Kim talks as shown in Figure 9 (a). For the decoder, we feed H.264 encoded video frames with the above sample content so that it periodically decompresses them to YUV raw video frames for display. This resembles the incoming video flow of a video phone call. For the encoder, we feed YUV raw video frames with the above sample content so that it periodically compresses them to H.264 encoded video frames for transmission. This resembles the outgoing video flow of a video phone call.

Figure 10 shows the result of our per-task analysis for the two tasks, that is, the decoder and encoder. For example, consider the decoder case when the RAM partition size S 1 = 37 (see the boxed graph of the decoder case). The graph shows that if the RAM partition is used only by LRU, the average execution time of the decoder task is 54.8 ms. On the other hand, if the same size RAM partition is used by the optimal pinning/LRU combination, the average execution time is reduced to 26.7 ms. This observation validates that the optimal pinning/LRU combination can really make a significant reduction of the execution time for the same size RAM partition. The similar observation can be made for the encoder case as well. Such optimal The resulting total RAM size by mRT-PLRU is reported in Figure 11. In the figure, we compare the required total RAM sizes by the following five methods:

• Shadowing: It is the traditional way to preload all the program code pages into RAM and execute the codes from RAM. • Shared LRU: It represents the default RAM usage provided by the original Linux OS where all the tasks share the entire RAM space using LRU-based demand-paging. For this method, due to unpredictable inter-task conflicts in the shared RAM, there is no known solution for determining the required RAM size for the probabilistic deadline guarantee. Thus, we report only a rough conservative estimation of the required RAM size. It is computed as follows:

(1) For a given size of shared RAM, we obtain the execution time distribution of the decoder assuming that the RAM contents loaded by the previous job of the decoder are maximally evicted by the encoder execution and hence the next job of the decoder should reload them when it tries to access the evicted pages. avoid the inter-task RAM conflicts where the same size RAM partitions are allocated to the encoder and decoder. Each task uses its assigned partition using only LRU. • Even-partitioned PLRU: It is the same as the evenpartitioned LRU except that each RAM partition is used by the optimal pinning/LRU combination. This method is considered to see the improvement by applying only the idea of pinning/LRU combination. • Our mRT-PLRU: It is our proposed method. It makes the improvement by applying both ideas of (1) pinning/LRU combination and (2) convex optimization based RAM allocation.

Figure 11 compares the above five methods in terms of the required total RAM size for different deadline meet probability requirements, P rob th = 90%, P rob th = 95%, and P rob th = 99%. Regardless of P rob th , the shadowing approach requires a large RAM size to preload all the code pages of the decoder and encoder programs. This size is significantly larger than those required by the other four methods, i.e., shared LRU, even-partitioned LRU, even-partitioned PLRU, and mRT-PLRU, because the shadowing approach needs to copy all the NAND code pages into RAM even though a large portion of them are very rarely accessed. On the other hand, the other four methods determines the RAM size based on the actual page reference traces and hence require a much smaller RAM size. All of the latter four methods require increasing RAM sizes as P rob th increases because the number of page faults needs to be smaller to meet a higher P rob th . For each value of P rob th , comparing the shared LRU and even-partitioned LRU, the figure shows the latter requires a smaller RAM. However, this may be because of our conservative estimation of the required RAM size for the shared LRU. If there were an accurate method to estimate it, it may be smaller than the required RAM size by the even-partitioned LRU. However, the problem is that there is no concrete method to estimate the required RAM size for the shared LRU. The gap between the even-partitioned LRU and even-partitioned PLRU shows the RAM reduction only with the pinning/LRU combination. In addition, the gap between the even-partitioned PLRU and mRT-PLRU shows the further RAM reduction by the convex-optimization based RAM allocation. By applying both (1) pinning/LRU combination and (2) convex-optimization based RAM allocation, the overall RAM saves by our mRT-PLRU compared to the traditional shadowing approach are 80%, 78%, and 75% for the cases of P rob th = 90%, P rob th = 95%, and P rob th = 99%, respectively.

In order to confirm that the optimal mRT-PLRU obtained with a sample video content can actually meet the requirement P rob th for real video contents, we perform trace-driven simulations with our mRT-PLRU configuration for other two video phone contents called "Content A" (Figure 9 (b) where Duhee Lee talks) and "Content B" (Figure 9 (c) where O-chul Kwon talks) and measure the deadline meet probabilities of the decoder and encoder tasks. For the two contents, Figure 12 shows the deadline meet probabilities of the lower priority task, i.e., the encoder, as increasing P rob th . The figure says that our mRT-PLRU configured with the sample content can also handle In order to justify the mRT-PLRU in terms of the quality that human actually perceives, we actually implement it by modifying the Linux's paging mechanism. Figure 13 shows our implementation results. To investigate the userperceived quality, we measured inter-frame gaps while the decoder and encoder are handling the video stream. 13(c) and (d) compare them for "Content B". The fluctuation of the inter-frame gaps by our mRT-PLRU is quite comparable to that of the shadowing. This order of differences are not perceivable by human.
In order to investigate the cases of more than two tasks, we consider the following five tasks:

• τ 1 : The above used decoder task with period 41.6 ms • τ 2 : The above used encoder task with period 41.6 ms • τ 3 : An artificially made task with period 80 ms. For modeling its j-th job, its execution time is assumed to be the same as that of j-th job of the decoder task. However, the job's page reference sequence is obtained from that of the j-th decoder job by swapping 10% randomly selected pairs of referenced pages. To model a different program, the pages in such a randomly perturbed sequence are assumed to be different ones from the pages used by the decoder task. • τ 4 : An artificially made task with period 120 ms. It is modeled just like τ 3 except 20% random perturbation for the page reference sequences. • τ 5 : An artificially made task with period 240 ms. It is modeled just like τ 3 except 30% random perturbation for the page reference sequences.

Figure 14 compares the required total RAM sizes by the shadowing and mRT-PLRU. As the number of tasks increases, the required total RAM sizes also increase for both methods. However, the increasing ratio for mRT-PLRU is much smaller than the shadowing, which enlarges the gap between them. This is because mRT-PLRU adds only the necessary size RAM partition for the probabilistic deadline guarantee of a newly added task, while the shadowing adds a large amount of RAM to hold the entire program code of the newly added task.

div.head: V. Related Work
div.p: Recently, there has been much work on software technologies considering physical characteristics of NAND flash memory. For example, JFFS [29] and YAFFS [17] are file systems specially designed for NAND flash memory. [11], [6], [10] are studies on how to use buffering, stripping, and pipelining mechanisms in order to maximize the NAND throughput by hiding its physical characteristics. [18], [19] discuss about the virtual memory systems based on NAND-aware demand-paging. However, none of these studies address the issues of satisfying real-time requirements.

Targeting real-time systems employing NAND flash memory, [7], [9] present special garbage collection techniques that make NAND write operations predictable even with the erase-before-write constraint. However, they focus on only write operations not the page-based read operations. Our previous work [12] addresses the issue of the page-based read operations in terms of probabilistically guaranteeing real-time program executions. However, the proposed technique called RT-PLRU is designed specifically targeting for a portable media player where only a single real-time program runs at a time. Thus, it is not applicable to generic multi-tasking real-time systems.

The problem of using RAM as working memory for executing codes in NAND flash memory is theoretically similar to the classical idea of using the cache for speedingup main memory accesses. In order to minimize the impact of cache-miss penalties, there are thousands of studies using different techniques, e.g., prefetching [2], branch prediction [21], and code placement [24]. However, most of work focuses on maximizing the cache-hit ratio rather than guaranteeing real-time performance. In the real-time community, there have been great efforts to make the cache performance predictable. Cache-locking [26], [5] and scratchpad memory [23], [27] try to make the cache behavior predictable by loading and locking a set of data into on-chip memory (cache or scratchpad memory). However, they require compile-time analysis or programmer's input to select the data set to be locked, which is not developer-transparent. The techniques in [1], [16] analyze the cache impact on the WCET without touching the cache behavior. However, they do not take into account cache misses by other tasks in multi-tasking environments. Targeting for multi-tasking environments, [4], [15] present techniques for bounding the the worst case delay in the cache due to preemptions. Those techniques, however, are developed based on the worst-case static analysis for hard real-time systems. Therefore, they involve tremendous pessimism if applied to soft real-time systems where cache access patterns widely vary depending on program inputs. In order to avoid inter-task conflicts in the cache, cachepartitioning techniques [13], [28], [3] partition the cache so that each task uses only its assigned partition. The idea is similar to our RAM partitioning. However, they do not consider the possible improvement by combining pinning and LRU in each partition. In summary, none of the above cache-related ideas can be trivially applied for building a developer-transparent framework to use NAND flash memory for soft real-time program executions in multitasking embedded systems.

div.head: VI. Conclusion
div.p: This paper presents a generic framework to use NAND flash memory for real-time program executions with the minimal usage of expensive RAM in multi-tasking environments. For the developer-transparency, the framework relies on the kernel configurator that automatically and optimally configures RAM. The optimal RAM configuration called mRT-PLRU determines the optimal allocation of RAM partitions to multiple tasks and also the optimal pinning/LRU combination for each RAM partition such that all the concurrent real-time tasks can probabilistically meet their deadlines with the minimum size of total RAM. Our experimental study conducted with realistic mobile video phone applications shows that the proposed mRT-PLRU can significantly reduce the total RAM requirement compared to the most commonly used shadowing approach.

Although the proposed technique opens an era of using NAND flash memory as a program code storage for realtime executions, there still remains several open issues to make the framework complete. First, we have to properly resolve the system bus conflicts by NAND accesses and other I/O devices requests. Second, for battery operated mobile embedded devices, we have to optimally trade-off the RAM cost and energy consumption. Finally, we need to extend the technique targeting for hard real-time systems.
All of these open issues will be addressed in our future work.
